newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Vienna councillor thrust into finance spotlight.
newsitem.headline: Vienna councillor thrust into finance spotlight.

text.p: Austria's new finance minister Rudolf Edlinger is a little-known regional politician who has been thrust into the toughest job in the coalition government.

Edlinger, 56, a Social Democrat, has controlled the purse strings of Vienna City Council since November 1994, overseeing an annual budget of 134 billion schillings ($11.7 billion), but he has no track record at national level.

The portly professional lithographer reluctantly answered chancellor-in-waiting Viktor Klima's call on Friday to move into the treasury hot seat and attempt to steer Austria's wayward economy into European Economic and Monetary Union.
Just 24 hours earlier, he had insisted he was not interested in the post, left open by Klima's sudden promotion to chancellor at the weekend.
"I am bowing to an urgent request from the chancellor that I could not possibly refuse," Edlinger, a heavy smoker and dedicated beer drinker, told Austrian radio after his appointment.
"I will tackle this difficult task with the necessary energy. I will take it on with optimism."
Edlinger, who was described by political commentators as quiet and unassuming, promised to bring pragmatism to the finance ministry after 30 years in local government.

He will need all his political savvy for crucial budget negotiations with the People's Party, the junior coalition partner. A stalemate over setting the 1996 budget forced the left-right coalition into early elections two years ago.
"I am not afraid of anyone. I work on basic principles, creating a climate for debate and seeking opinions to solve problems," said Edlinger, the father of three.
The son of a Vienna type-setter and an ardent fan of Rapid Vienna soccer team, he was not Klima's first choice to take over the fiscal reins.

Klima had sought to persuade Social Democratic leader Karl Stix, head of the Burgenland regional government, to move to Vienna. His efforts foundered on the refusal of Burgenland People's Party to guarantee its support for a Social Democrat replacement for Stix.
Klima responded with irritation to suggestions that Edlinger was a poor second choice.

He expressed confidence that Edlinger, supported by new State Secretary for Finance Wolfgang Ruttenstorfer, a former board member of OMV oil company, would rise to the challenge of preparing Austria for a single European currency in 1999.
"There were two outstanding candidates for finance minister. The combination of Edlinger and Ruttenstorfer is an excellent choice," he said.
In his newly-created post, Ruttenstorfer, 46, will concentrate on issues connected with European Economic and Monetary Union and capital markets, Klima said.
"Vienna is losing an outstanding finance chief and Austria is gaining an excellent finance minister," Vienna mayor Michael Haeupl said of Edlinger.
Secretary general Peter Westenthaler of the opposition far-right Freedom Party countered: "Klima has appointed a cabinet of apparatchiks."
